title: Time, days & months
goal: Tell and ask the time, name the days and months, and talk about today, yesterday, tomorrow and parts of the day.
intro:
Telugu tells the time in *గంటలు* (gaṇṭalu, hours, literally 'bells') with handy words for quarters and halves: *మూడుంబావు* (quarter past three), *మూడున్నర* (half past three). Note the special form for one o'clock: *ఒంటి గంట* (oṇṭi gaṇṭa).

Days of the week are named after the planets (*సోమ*, moon; *మంగళ*, Mars...) and all end in *-వారం* (vāram). For months, the English names are used in daily life.

phrases.en: I'll be there in five minutes.
I'm a bit late. (lit. a little delay happened)
I went to Hyderabad last month.
I go to bed at ten at night.

grammar.title: Telling the time
grammar.body:
Ask **ఇప్పుడు టైం ఎంత?** (what's the time now?) or **ఎన్ని గంటలైంది?** (enni gaṇṭalaindi?, how many hours has it become?).

Answer with number + **గంటలు**: *మూడు గంటలు* (3:00). One o'clock is special: **ఒంటి గంట** (oṇṭi gaṇṭa).
Quarter past: number + **-ంబావు**: మూడుంబావు (3:15)
Half past: number + **-న్నర**: మూడున్నర (3:30)
Quarter to: next hour + **-కి పావు తక్కువ**: నాలుగుకి పావు తక్కువ (3:45)
Minutes: మూడు గంటల పది నిమిషాలు (3:10)

'At' a time is the dative **-కి**: *ఐదు గంటలకి* (at five). Parts of the day go first: *సాయంత్రం ఆరు గంటలకి* (at 6 p.m.). In cities, English times ('six-thirty') are very common.

examples.en: The train comes at quarter past five.

grammar.title: Days, months and time expressions
grammar.body:
Days need no 'on': *సోమవారం వస్తాను* (I'll come on Monday). Months take **-లో** (in): *మేలో* (in May). The months in everyday use are English: జనవరి, ఫిబ్రవరి, మార్చి, ఏప్రిల్, మే, జూన్, జులై, ఆగస్టు, సెప్టెంబరు, అక్టోబరు, నవంబరు, డిసెంబరు. Traditional Telugu months (చైత్రం, వైశాఖం ...) are used for festivals and auspicious dates.

**తర్వాత** (after) and **ముందు** (before) follow a noun: *భోజనం తర్వాత*. 'Ago' is **కిందట**: *రెండు రోజుల కిందట* (two days ago). **వచ్చే** (coming) = next, **పోయిన** (gone) = last: *వచ్చే నెల*, *పోయిన వారం*. 'Within/in' a time is **-లో**: *ఐదు నిమిషాల్లో*.

examples.en: On Monday I go to the office.
After lunch I lie down for a bit.

dialogue.title: Finding a time to meet
dialogue.setting: Anil and Divya, classmates, try to fix a time to work on a project.

lines.speaker: Divya
lines.native: రేపు గురువారం కదా? పొద్దున్న నాకు క్లాసు ఉంది.
lines.roman: rēpu guruvāram kadā? poddunna nāku klāsu undi.
lines.en: Tomorrow's Thursday, right? I have class in the morning.

lines.speaker: Anil
lines.en: Then shall we meet at half past three?

lines.speaker: Anil
lines.en: At the coffee shop near the college.

lines.speaker: Divya
lines.en: Fine, half three. Don't be late!

lines.speaker: Anil
lines.en: No, no, I'll be on time.

culture: The Telugu New Year, *ఉగాది* (Ugadi), falls in March–April at the start of the lunar month *చైత్రం*, and is celebrated with *ఉగాది పచ్చడి*, a chutney mixing six tastes for the joys and sorrows of the year ahead. *సంక్రాంతి* in January is the great harvest festival. Many families still consult the *పంచాంగం* (almanac) for an auspicious time (*ముహూర్తం*) before weddings or moving house, and 'Indian Standard Time' jokes about lateness are common.
